copy_visibility_reason: The bloom and the hammered bar are visible, and a bloomery can be watched at work, but the ore choice, the charcoal ratio and the feel for when the bloom is ready stay in the smith's hands.
name: Wrought iron (bloomery)
note: Already produced at scale wherever there is a strong ironworking tradition (Noricum is famous for supplying Rome's). Soft, tough, weldable, no useful casting.

copy_visibility_reason: The alloy colour and the casting are visible, but the tin share is not, and a founder cannot read it off the finished piece without assay.
name: Bronze
note: Bronze is copper alloyed with tin, harder than copper alone and easy to cast, and it is already made wherever casters know the craft. It is melted in a crucible, poured into a mould and finished by hand. It supplies castings, bearings, statuary and instruments. The limit is the supply of tin, which must be hauled from far away, and the quality of the mould.

copy_visibility_reason: The golden metal shows nothing of the calamine and charcoal packed round the copper, and no onlooker sees that a second metal went in.
name: Brass (by cementation)
note: Already made wherever copper is heated with calamine and charcoal, without anyone ever seeing zinc metal. See mat_zinc for why.

name: Lead
note: Already available in enormous quantity wherever there is a major lead-mining region (Britannia and Hispania supply Rome's). Cheap. The only common material that survives hot sulfuric acid.

name: Tin
note: Tin is a soft, low-melting metal that is mixed with copper to make bronze and used to coat other metals. It is already available wherever there is trade access to a source; Rome's comes from Cornwall and Iberia. Tin ore is found in few places, so it is expensive and travels a long way by sea and river, and a cut trade route leaves bronze makers short of it.

name: Copper (fire refined)
note: Poling and fire refining to get copper clean enough to draw into long fine wire without breaking. A separate node from electro-refining because you need it before you have any electricity.

name: Silver
note: Silver is won from galena, which is first smelted to a silver-bearing lead. That lead is then heated in air in a shallow cup of porous bone ash (a cupel): the lead oxidises to litharge, which soaks into the cup, while the silver does not oxidise and stays behind as a bead. It needs a hot furnace with a steady air blast and careful heat control, and it is already practised wherever cupellation from galena is known.

name: Gold
note: Gold is a soft, dense, heavy yellow metal that does not tarnish, so it is used for coin, ornament and as a store of wealth. It is already mined wherever there is a working goldfield; Rome's include Las Medulas in Spain, and Dacia from 106 AD. It is won by washing gold-bearing gravel or by crushing and processing ore, and the mines belong to the state, so the founder gets it by trade or concession.

name: Mercury
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a cinnabar source (Rome's is Almaden, an imperial monopoly; Pliny NH 33.118 price-fixes minium at 70 HS per pound).

name: Sulfur
note: Sulfur is a yellow, brittle solid that burns with a choking blue flame. It is used to fumigate, to bleach, in medicines and, later, in black powder and sulfuric acid. It is already available wherever there is trade access to a volcanic source; Sicily and the Aeolian islands supply Rome's. It is dug from volcanic vents, so the founder depends on a distant supplier.

name: Natron (sodium carbonate)
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a natron source (Rome's is Wadi Natrun). IT IS NOT SALTPETRE. This confusion has wrecked more bootstrap plans than any other single error.

name: Quicklime and slaked lime
note: Quicklime is limestone heated in a kiln until it gives off carbon dioxide; slaked lime is quicklime mixed with water, which releases much heat. It is already produced wherever limestone is burned, and it needs a steady supply of fuel for the kiln. It serves as mortar, glass flux, causticising (making alkalis stronger) and a field dressing in agriculture. Quicklime burns skin and eyes, so it is handled with care.

name: Gypsum plaster
note: Gypsum is a soft white mineral (calcium sulfate with water locked in it). Heating it gently drives off some of that water to give plaster, which sets hard again when mixed with water. It is already available wherever there is a gypsum deposit. It is used for plaster, casting moulds and cement additives. Overheat it and it will no longer set properly.

name: Alum
note: Alum is a crystalline mineral salt that dissolves in water and is dug or boiled out of certain rocks. As a mordant it helps dye bind to cloth, so colours do not wash out. It also tightens tissue and can stop small bleeding, and it is used to size paper. Only a few places produce it, so reaching an alum source by trade is what makes it available.

name: Vitriols (iron and copper sulfates)
note: Already lying in heaps at pyrite mines as a weathering product everywhere pyrite is worked, and generally nobody yet has any idea what it is for. Feedstock for sulfuric acid.

name: Pyrolusite (manganese dioxide)
note: Already mined and already used as glassmaker's soap, wherever there is a live glass industry, generally without anyone knowing why it works.

name: Galena (lead sulfide)
note: Already available everywhere lead is mined. It is also a working semiconductor, which nobody will suspect for 1800 years.

name: Calamine (zinc carbonate/silicate ore)
note: Calamine is a zinc ore (a carbonate or a silicate). Heated with copper and charcoal, the zinc is absorbed into the copper to make brass, without ever being melted off as a separate metal. It is already mined and made into brass wherever both ore and the skill exist. Free zinc metal cannot be produced this way, because zinc vapour escapes and burns.

name: Asbestos
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a deposit (Rome's is Cyprus; Pliny describes it). Useful, and it will kill your workers slowly.

name: Emery (Naxos)
note: Emery is a naturally occurring very hard grit of corundum (aluminium oxide) mixed with iron minerals, used crushed as an abrasive to grind and polish metal, glass and stone. It is already available wherever there is trade access to a deposit; the famous source is the Greek island of Naxos. It is the founder's abrasive for every ground surface, and the supply of it limits fine grinding.

name: Pozzolana and hydraulic concrete
note: Pozzolanic reaction between silica and lime happens slowly and imperceptibly. The concrete is weak for months then becomes very hard. No chemical knowledge, only empirical observation of ash quality and mixing ratio.

name: Papyrus
note: Papyrus is a writing sheet made from the pith of a Nile reed: strips are laid crosswise, wetted and pressed, and the plant's own sap glues them as they dry. It never becomes pulp, so it works fresh and wet and does not cure with paste. It needs reeds from Egypt and a flat press. It is cheap and smooth but brittle, cannot be erased well and rots in damp climates.

name: Parchment
note: Parchment is a writing surface made from animal skin that is unhaired, scraped and dried under tension but never tanned. It accepts ink, and mistakes can be scraped off and rewritten. The skin is soaked in a lime bath to loosen the hair: too much lime dissolves the fibre, too little leaves hair. It needs skins, lime, scraping knives and a frame, and costs far more per page than papyrus.

copy_visibility_reason: Retting ponds, scutching and hackling are done in the open and each step shows its result; the retting time and water that spare the fibre are learned by doing.
name: Linen
note: Linen is cloth made from flax fibre. The stalks are retted (soaked so microbes rot the pectin gluing fibre to the woody core), broken and scutched to free the long fibres, hackled (combed) to clean and align them, then spun and woven. It is already produced routinely wherever flax is grown and processed.

name: Wool
note: ROME HAS THIS.

copy_visibility_reason: The tanyard and its pits are visible and smell far off, but the strength and timing of the tanning liquors, which decide the leather, are not visible.
name: Leather
note: Leather is animal skin tanned with plant tannins or minerals so that it no longer rots and stays flexible. It is already produced wherever livestock are kept and tanned, and it needs hides, tanning vats and a supply of tannin from bark or galls, and time. Tanning is slow and the vats smell badly. The founder uses it for bellows, seals, gaskets and drive belts.

name: Beeswax
note: Beeswax is a wax made by honeybees to build their combs, solid at room temperature and soft when warm. It is already available wherever bees are kept, collected when honey is taken and melted clean. It is used in lost wax casting (a wax model is coated in clay, melted out and replaced by metal), in luting (sealing joints) and as an acid-proof coating. The supply depends on bee keepers.

name: Tallow
note: Tallow is hard animal fat, rendered by heating fatty tissue and straining the liquid. It is already available wherever animals are rendered. It burns in candles and, more importantly for the founder, it lubricates wire drawing and machining so that metal slides through dies and cutters without tearing. It goes rancid with time, so it must be fresh or well kept.

name: Olive oil
note: Olive oil is pressed from olives, crushing the fruit to a paste and squeezing it between mats or beams. It is already available in industrial quantity wherever olives are grown at scale. It serves as food, lamp fuel, soap base, quenching oil for tempering steel and a varnish base. It needs groves, presses and containers, and a poor harvest cuts the supply for every use at once.

name: Bitumen and naphtha seeps
note: Already available wherever there is trade access to a seep (Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea supply Rome's). Cable insulation, waterproofing, and the seed of petroleum chemistry.

name: Salt
note: Already available, taxed and strategically controlled, wherever there is a salt works. Feedstock for hydrochloric acid and the whole chlor-alkali branch.

copy_visibility_reason: Clear glass shows nothing of the batch, the ash or sand choice or the annealing; Venetian glassmakers were bound by law not to leave Murano, which shows the recipe was worth guarding.
name: Soda-lime glass
note: Already made, and made well, wherever there is a live glass industry, including deliberately decolourised near-colourless glass.

name: Charcoal
note: Charcoal is wood heated in a pile or kiln with too little air for it to burn, leaving nearly pure carbon that burns hotter and cleaner than wood. It is already produced wherever wood is burned for it. Smelting metal and firing glass all need it. The real ceiling on iron output is forest, not ore, because a furnace consumes enormous amounts of fuel and trees regrow slowly.

name: Silk (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT RUINOUS. Silk Road via Palmyra. Pliny complains of the bullion drain east. Your best early wire insulation.

name: Shellac (traded)
note: REACHABLE BUT DEAR. Indian Ocean trade via Berenice to Muziris, 1 to 3 year lead time. Your best varnish and the only good coil insulation you will have for a century.

name: Natural rubber
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Hevea is Amazonian, but Landolphia and Funtumia vines in West and Central Africa yield real rubber and were the basis of a large industry in the 1890s. West Africa is COASTAL SAILING from the Pillars of Hercules and Hanno the Carthaginian did it around 500 BC. You need a voyage down a coast and the knowledge of which vine to tap, not an ocean crossing.

name: Gutta percha
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Palaquium latex from Malaya, reached by extending east whatever long-distance ocean trade route you already have (Rome already sails there annually). Indian and Malay traders already carry it partway.

name: Quinine from cinchona
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, only Andean. Malaria is endemic across much of the Mediterranean and the tropical world, which makes this worth an ocean crossing by itself wherever it is a problem for you. Once you have it, TRANSPLANT it: the Dutch and British both moved cinchona out of Peru and broke the monopoly.

name: Sodium nitrate
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, and also not needed. Bengal saltpetre is already on a trade route reachable by long-distance sea trade (Rome's India route is one example) and supplied the world's gunpowder for centuries, and nitre beds work anywhere. The Chilean desert deposits are real and reachable the same way potato and cacao are, but you will not need them.

name: New World crops
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. These are CROPS, not commodities, out of the Americas: you need seed stock once and then you grow them forever. One successful voyage home with potato seed changes the caloric ceiling of agriculture permanently.

name: Cryolite, or a synthetic fluoride bath
unheld_reason: Greenland cryolite is mined from the 1850s
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE, and the interesting part is that you should not go and get it. Ivigtut in Greenland is the only workable natural deposit and reaching it is a North Atlantic voyage far harder than anything else in this tree. The synthetic route is easier: cryolite is sodium aluminium fluoride, and you can make the bath from hydrofluoric acid, which you get by warming fluorspar with sulfuric acid. Fluorspar occurs in Britain and the Alps. The catch is that HF attacks glass, so it must be handled in lead or wax-lined vessels, and it does something worse to people: it penetrates skin painlessly and destroys bone calcium hours later. Treat every splash as serious even when it does not hurt.

name: Platinum
note: NOT UNOBTAINABLE. Colombian and Ural placers. The Urals are reachable overland through Scythian and Sarmatian trade without crossing any ocean. Take the overland road: extend the eastern trade routes and buy Ural placer metal from the people who already work it. Rounding the Cape for the Colombian placers will also get you there, at far greater cost.

copy_visibility_reason: Castings and the tapping of a furnace are visible, but the burden, blast and slag control that keep a furnace running are hidden in the operation.
name: Cast iron
note: Brittle, cheap, castable, 3-4% carbon. Rome has none in the West; Han China has had it for 500 years. Pipes, pots, cannon, machine frames, stoves.

name: Blister steel
note: Bar iron packed in charcoal at about 1000 C for days. Carbon penetrates on the order of a millimetre a day, so use thin bars.

name: Crucible steel
note: Homogeneous, slag-free, and the gate on every cutting tool and every lead screw.

copy_visibility_reason: A converter blow is a spectacle anyone can watch, but the lining chemistry and the phosphorus in the ore are invisible; early Bessemer licensees failed on phosphoric ores until the cause was understood.
name: Bulk steel (converter and open hearth)
note: Cheap steel in thousands of tonnes rather than kilogrammes. Note the phosphorus problem: acid linings cannot remove it and most European ores contain it, so you need the basic lining (Thomas and Gilchrist) with a dolomite hearth. Missing this cost Bessemer years, and knowing it in advance saves you them. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down.

mine_works.source: temporary_heuristic: steel edge rail and wire-rope haulage underground. Load per carrier trip = a horse's sustained pull (about 500 N, a heuristic) over rolling resistance times gravity, one driver per train, speed as the barrow's. Edge-rail resistance is taken at 0.01, so about 5 tonnes.

name: High speed and alloy tool steel
note: Tool steel that keeps its hardness when it gets red hot, because it contains tungsten and chromium that form hard carbides (compounds of metal with carbon). It is made in a hot furnace from tungsten, chromium and analysed carbon steel. Cutting tools of ordinary steel soften at high cutting speeds; these do not, so every machine tool can cut much faster and its output rises greatly.

name: Stainless steel
note: Stainless steel is steel with enough chromium (above about eleven per cent) that its surface forms a thin, self-healing layer of chromium oxide that stops rust. It needs pure chromium, a very hot furnace and precise analysis to hit the right composition. It does not corrode, so it serves chemical plant, cutlery and vacuum systems, but it is hard to forge and machine.

copy_visibility_reason: The metal reaches a buyer as ingots and shows nothing of the sealed retort and downward condensing; European users imported zinc from the East before they could make it.
name: Zinc metal
note: CRITICAL PATH AND ALMOST NOBODY SEES IT. Zinc boils at 907 C, below the temperature at which its ore is reduced, so the metal leaves as vapour and reburns at the furnace mouth. That is exactly why brass gets made by cementation everywhere, without anyone having seen the metal itself. Seal the retort and condense downward. No zinc, no voltaic pile, no electricity.

name: Nickel
note: Nickel was not isolated in antiquity, because its ores are hard to smelt and are easily mistaken for copper ores. It is won by roasting and smelting the ore to a metal-rich matte and refining that, by chemical routes such as the Mond process (a gas that carries nickel off as a vapour) or by electrolytic refining, and needs very high heat and chemical purification. It is used for coinage, plating, alloy steels, glass-to-metal seals and catalysts.

name: Chromium
note: Chromium is a hard, bright metal that resists corrosion, obtained from chromite ore by reducing it, either with aluminium powder (aluminothermic) or with carbon at very high temperature. It needs the electric furnace for high heat and quantitative analysis to control the product. It is the alloying element of stainless steel and is used for plating and furnace linings (refractories).

name: Manganese and ferromanganese
note: Deoxidises and desulfurises steel. Already mined as a glass decolouriser in any developed glass industry (Rome among them), without anyone yet realising it is a metal.

name: Tungsten
note: Melts at 3422 C, the highest of any metal. Lamp filaments, high speed steel, carbide tooling. Needs the arc furnace or hydrogen reduction of the oxide followed by powder sintering.

copy_visibility_reason: The grey metal shows nothing of the bath or the current; an onlooker at the cell sees molten salt and glow but not the bath composition or the cell control.
name: Aluminium
note: Hall-Heroult in a molten fluoride bath. Cryolite is Greenlandic and unobtainable, so you must synthesise the bath from your own hydrofluoric acid. Before electricity aluminium is a precious metal; after it, it is roofing.

name: Magnesium
note: Magnesium is a very light metal, made by passing electric current through molten magnesium chloride so that metal collects at one electrode and chlorine at the other. It needs cheap grid electricity and an industrial electrochemistry plant. It makes light alloys and a brilliant white flash powder for photography, and it is a powerful reducing agent. Magnesium burns fiercely, so fires are a hazard.

name: High purity graphite
note: Acheson process: heat carbon to about 2500 C. Crucibles and boats that do not contaminate what is melted in them, which is exactly what zone refining needs.

name: Carbon black and lampblack
note: Already produced wherever lamps or fires are burned for soot. Ink pigment, and much later the reinforcing filler that makes rubber into tyres.

name: Lead crystal (flint glass)
note: High dispersion. Pair it with crown glass and you get the achromatic doublet, which is what makes a compound microscope beat a single bead.

name: Borosilicate glass
note: Low thermal expansion. The difference between a laboratory and a pile of broken retorts. Needs boron; the Larderello fumaroles in Tuscany are inside the Empire, which is a genuinely lucky break if it holds.

name: Fused quartz
note: Pure silica worked at 1700 to 2000 C with an oxy-hydrogen flame. Indispensable later: you cannot zone refine germanium in anything that contaminates it.

copy_visibility_reason: Europe imported Chinese porcelain for centuries and could not copy it until Bottger's work in the early 1700s; the white body, the kaolin and the high firing are invisible in the finished ware.
name: Porcelain and high-fired stoneware
unheld_reason: Han high-fired stoneware is not yet porcelain; needs a historian
note: Kaolin plus feldspar at about 1300 C. Chemical ware, electrical insulators, and an extremely profitable luxury export that Europe chased for six centuries.

copy_visibility_reason: The grey powder shows nothing of the limestone and clay ratio or the burning temperature, and Aspdin kept his recipe secret when he patented it.
name: Portland cement
note: Calcined limestone and clay, ground fine. HONEST NOTE: it is not obviously better than Roman pozzolanic concrete for marine work. Its advantage is consistency and independence from Puteoli.

name: Reinforced concrete
note: Roman concrete is superb in compression and useless in tension. Steel rod fixes that, and the thermal expansion of steel and concrete happen to match closely enough to work, which is luck rather than design.

copy_visibility_reason: The sheet shows its fibres but not the beating, sizing or mould work; tradition has the craft crossing into the Islamic world with captured papermakers, so it moved with people rather than samples.
name: Rag paper
note: Linen rags, retted, limed, beaten by a water-driven stamper, lifted on a wire mould. Cheaper than papyrus, far cheaper than parchment, and the substrate of everything in the information branch.

name: Celluloid (nitrocellulose plastic)
note: Nitrocellulose becomes plastic when mixed with camphor. Sheet is then made by rolling between heated cylinders. Celluloid revolutionises photography by replacing glass plates, enables flexible film stock, and is used for combs, buttons, piano keys. The material is flammable and degrades over time to become increasingly brittle.

name: Camphor (traded)
note: Camphor is a waxy, strongly scented solid distilled from the wood of the camphor tree, which grows in east Asia. It is reachable only through the Indian Ocean and Chinese trade, and is expensive. The founder needs it to plasticise celluloid (an early plastic made from cellulose nitrate) and for some smokeless powders. Supply is thin and controlled by distant traders.

name: Bakelite (phenol formaldehyde)
note: The first fully synthetic plastic, from coal tar phenol. Electrical insulation, housings, and the thing that makes mass-produced electrical goods possible.

name: Formaldehyde
note: Formaldehyde is a pungent gas, made by passing methanol vapour mixed with air over a hot catalyst (a substance that speeds a reaction without being used up). The methanol comes from the destructive distillation of wood. It needs pure chemicals and a heated catalytic reactor. Dissolved in water it is the first practical tissue preservative, and it makes resins; it is toxic and irritates the lungs.

name: Synthetic rubber
note: YOUR ONLY ROUTE TO RUBBER. Butadiene from petroleum or from alcohol, polymerised. It sits behind a full petrochemical industry, which is why every plan that casually assumes rubber is wrong by about a century.

copy_visibility_reason: Kerosene and wax are visible products and a still can be seen at work, but cut points and the removal of impurities are matters of operating skill.
name: Refined petroleum fractions
note: Mesopotamian and Caucasian seeps are workable without drilling. Fractionate into naphtha, kerosene, gas oil, lubricants, wax and residue. Kerosene lighting alone pays for the plant.

name: Ammonia
note: Ammonia liquor is a by-product of coking coal, so it is nearly free once you coke. Fertiliser, refrigeration, nitric acid via Ostwald oxidation.

copy_visibility_reason: The bleached cloth and the smell are evident, but the generating plant, the absorption in lime and the handling of the gas are not shown by the product.
name: Chlorine and bleach
note: Bleaching powder ends the field-bleaching bottleneck that limited every textile industry, and hypochlorite makes water safe. Also war gas: be careful whom you teach.

copy_visibility_reason: The dyed cloth can be analysed by a trained chemist, but the route from coal tar through the intermediates and the plant that runs it are not visible; imitators needed their own chemists.
name: Synthetic dyes (aniline)
note: Coal tar to benzene to aniline to mauveine and the rest. Historically this single industry funded organic chemistry, created the first industrial research laboratories, and led directly to pharmaceuticals. Enormously profitable and politically harmless.

Reason: coal tar to aniline synthesis involves exothermic reactions needing temperature control]

copy_visibility_reason: The fibre looks unchanged after nitration, and the acid mix, temperature and the washing that decide whether it is stable are invisible; several early plants blew up for lack of it.
name: Nitrocellulose
note: Guncotton and the base of smokeless powder, celluloid and film. Unstable if badly washed; several early factories destroyed themselves.

name: Nitroglycerin and dynamite
note: Nitroglycerin is prepared by adding glycerol dropwise to a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acid at 10 C or below. It is a contact explosive - shock or friction detonates it with no need for a fuse. It is also unstable on storage and can spontaneously explode. Absorption onto diatomaceous earth (dynamite) is the only practical way to handle it safely.

name: Glycerol
note: A by-product of soap making that Rome throws away.

name: Artificial ice and mechanical refrigeration
note: Ammonia or ether evaporation in a compressor cools an ice chamber. Requires a steam engine to drive the compressor. Early mechanical ice-makers (Carve, 1850s) free wealthy households from dependence on natural ice harvesting and storage.
